title: Adastra : Technical Documentation
text:
0.1 Executive Summary
Adastra is an intelligent quantitative risk management and wealth advisory cockpit designed for the China A-shares equity market (~3,500 active listed companies). Built for the Shenzhen International FinTech Competition (FinTechathon 2026) : WeBank Track, the platform couples institutional quantitative finance, behavioral asset pricing, and natural language processing of Chinese financial news, with native compliance under the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) suitability guidelines.

They are strictly excluded from version control via .gitignore and are never exposed or transferred to the public web or cloud servers.

title: 2  System Architecture
text:
2.2 Layer 1: ML Pipeline (Offline Batch)
The quantitative engine runs offline to produce enriched prediction datasets. It is fully deterministic : zero LLM dependency for any financial computation.

2.2.1 Data Ingestion & Feature Engineering








Source File
Size
Content




features_light.parquet
243 MB
100+ fundamental accounting ratios for ~3,500 stocks × 12 years


news_embeddings_1024d.parquet
2.1 GB
1024-dimensional Chinese news transformer embeddings



Note: In accordance with our Zero-Data Policy and commercial database IP licenses, raw source datasets (China_Ashares_FC_and_NewsEmbedding.parquet, 2.1 GB) reside exclusively in a secured offline directory on the developer’s local Mac workstation. The public cloud deployment operates on synthetic calibrated benchmark data to prevent data leakage and theft.
Processing Pipeline:

Dimensionality Reduction (Look-Ahead Free): IncrementalPCA compresses 1024 news embedding dimensions -> 30 principal components (preserving >85% explained variance). To strictly eliminate look-ahead bias, the PCA model is fitted exclusively on historical training data (\(t < 2023\)), and subsequently used to transform both training and out-of-sample test embeddings.
Orthogonal Surprise Filtering: Ridge Regression of 10 PCA news dimensions onto 100 accounting characteristics extracts the residual \(\epsilon = \text{News} - \hat{\text{News}}\), isolating pure unexpected news surprise (Didisheim et al., 2026).
Behavioral Finance Features: Tversky-Kahneman Prospect Theory value function distance identifies 100 nearest psychological peers per stock, computing cross-asset momentum signals (tk_peer_reward).
Panic Signal Engineering: Interaction term \(\text{ivol} \times \max(0, -\text{ret})\) captures acute panic selling episodes.
Strict Temporal Alignment & Lagging: Predictors are aligned with rigorous temporal discipline (\(t-1\) relative to target returns) to eliminate look-ahead bias. Financial accounting characteristics natively incorporate reporting publication delays (4-month lag for quarterly reports, 6-month lag for annual statements).



2.2.2 Model Training & Inference

Algorithm: Cost-sensitive multiclass LightGBM with class_weight='balanced'
Hyperparameter Optimization: Optuna (Tree-structured Parzen Estimator), 15 Bayesian trials on temporal holdout (Train: 2018-2021, Val: 2022)
Validation: Expanding Walk-Forward protocol across 11 out-of-sample years (2012-2022)
Output: Calibrated 5-class posterior probabilities + exact TreeSHAP attribution vectors for every stock-month

title: 3  Core Algorithm Description
text:
3.1.1 Why Risk Classification Instead of Return Prediction?
Conventional point-return regression in quantitative finance suffers from near-zero signal-to-noise ratios. Monthly stock returns have standard deviations an order of magnitude larger than their means, making precise point estimates unreliable.
Our approach reformulates the problem as a 5-class risk classification aligned directly with CSRC (China Securities Regulatory Commission) investor suitability guidelines:

This formulation is not arbitrary : it directly maps to CSRC product risk ratings (R1 through R5), enabling seamless integration with the compliance engine. Each prediction carries immediate regulatory meaning.

title: 3  Core Algorithm Description
text:
3.2 Feature Engineering Pipeline

3.2.1 1. Orthogonal News Shocks (Didisheim et al., 2026)
Raw NLP text embeddings heavily duplicate information already present in financial statements. We decompose news signals into:
\[
\text{News}_{i,t} = \underbrace{\hat{\text{News}}_{i,t}}_{\text{Expected (priced by fundamentals)}} + \underbrace{\epsilon_{i,t}}_{\text{Orthogonal Surprise (News Shock)}}
\]
Procedure:

Embedding Compression: 1024-dimensional Chinese news transformer embeddings -> 30 principal components via IncrementalPCA (batch size = 5,000 for memory efficiency on 2.1 GB data)
Ridge Regression: For each of the top 10 PCA components, regress onto 100 accounting characteristics cross-sectionally
Residual Extraction: The orthogonal residual \(\epsilon_{i,t}\) represents the pure unexpected news surprise : information that was not already priced into the balance sheet

This innovation ensures our model captures genuinely new information rather than redundant financial statement echoes.


3.2.2 2. Behavioral Finance: TK Peer Reward (Barberis et al., 2016)
China A-shares are dominated by ~200 million retail investors who exhibit strong behavioral biases. We model this via Tversky-Kahneman Prospect Theory:
S-Shaped Value Function: \[
v(x) = \begin{cases}
x^{\alpha} & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\
-\lambda(-x)^{\beta} & \text{if } x < 0
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\alpha = \beta = 0.88\) and \(\lambda \approx 2.25\) (loss aversion coefficient).
Peer Identification: For each stock \(i\), we compute the Prospect Theory value function over its trailing 60-month return distribution, then identify the 100 nearest psychological peers : stocks whose historical return “feel” is most similar to retail investors.
TK Peer Reward: The cross-sectional average return of these 100 peers serves as a behavioral momentum signal, capturing sentiment contagion effects across psychologically similar assets.


3.2.3 3. Non-Linear Panic Signal
Standard volatility measures treat positive and negative returns symmetrically. We engineer an asymmetric panic indicator:
\[
\text{Panic}_{i,t} = \text{ivol}_{i,t} \times \max(0, -\text{ret}_{i,t-1})
\]
This interaction term captures acute panic selling episodes where high volatility coincides with recent negative momentum : a pattern that precedes severe crash regimes.

title: 3  Core Algorithm Description
text:
3.3 Model Architecture

3.3.1 LightGBM Multiclass Classifier
We use Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (LightGBM) for several reasons:

Tabular data superiority: GBDTs consistently outperform neural networks on structured financial data
Interpretability: Native exact TreeSHAP computation without approximation
Speed: Handles 770,000+ observations with 100+ features efficiently
Cost-sensitivity: class_weight='balanced' addresses severe class imbalance (crash events are rare)



3.3.2 Hyperparameter Optimization (Optuna)
Rather than arbitrary parameters or grid search, we use Bayesian optimization via Optuna’s Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE):

title: 3  Core Algorithm Description
text:
3.4 Temporal Validation Protocol

3.4.1 Why Not K-Fold Cross-Validation?
Random K-Fold shuffling is invalid in quantitative finance because it introduces severe look-ahead bias: the model can “see” future data during training, inflating performance metrics artificially.


3.4.2 Expanding Walk-Forward Validation (2012-2022)
For every test year \(T \in [2012, 2022]\):

Training data: All years strictly before \(T\) (i.e., \(< T\))
Test data: Year \(T\) only
No overlap: Zero information leakage between training and test

This validates model robustness across 11 distinct market regimes:

title: 3  Core Algorithm Description
text:
3.5 Explainable AI (TreeSHAP)

3.5.1 Exact SHAP Values
For every stock-month observation in the 2023 test set (35,085 observations), we compute exact TreeSHAP values : not approximations.
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) decomposes each prediction into additive feature contributions:
\[
f(x) = \phi_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{M} \phi_j
\]
where \(\phi_0\) is the base value and \(\phi_j\) is the contribution of feature \(j\) to pushing the prediction away from the baseline.


3.5.2 Natural Language Synthesis
The top 5 SHAP drivers for each stock are translated into intuitive natural language via the xai.py module. The synthesis engine:

Separates features into risk-increasing (\(\phi_j > 0\)) and risk-mitigating (\(\phi_j < 0\)) groups
Maps technical feature names to human-readable descriptions (e.g., ivol_capm_252d -> “long-term market volatility”)
Generates category-specific explanations calibrated to the stock’s risk classification
Appends Kahneman-Tversky Tail-Risk Guardrail warnings when crash probability exceeds 15%

3.6.2 Performance Summary (Gross & Net of Transaction Costs)
To ensure academic and institutional rigor, backtest performance is evaluated both gross and net of realistic transaction friction. In China A-shares, institutional trading encounters stamp duty (0.05% on sells), brokerage commissions (~0.025%), and bid-ask slippage (~0.10%), representing an estimated ~20 bps round-trip friction per monthly rebalance.






NoteCrucial Methodological Clarification: “Equal-Weighted ML Universe” vs Market-Cap Indices (e.g., CSI 300)



The benchmark reported in our backtest is the Equal-Weighted ML Universe Benchmark, defined as the cross-sectional arithmetic mean return of all active China A-share equities evaluated by the model in each month (\(R_{\text{benchmark}, t} = \frac{1}{N_t} \sum_{i=1}^{N_t} r_{i,t}\)).
It is not a capitalization-weighted equity index like the CSI 300. In calendar year 2023, while the capitalization-weighted CSI 300 index fell by -11.38% (weighed down by mega-cap state-owned enterprises, real estate developers, and traditional banking giants), the broader equal-weighted cross-section of active A-shares exhibited positive returns (+8.27% on the active news-covered universe of 24,209 stock-months, and +4.60% across the comprehensive 37,247 stock-month universe). Benchmarking against the exact investable universe from which the model selects assets eliminates selection bias and strictly adheres to CFA Institute / GIPS institutional performance presentation standards.

TipKey Insight: Asymmetric Downside Avoidance



Even after deducting full transaction friction and execution slippage (-2.0% to -2.4% annual drag), the Opportunity Strategy achieves +12.06% net cumulative return (Sharpe 1.03).
The primary driver is the asymmetric avoidance of catastrophic downside: the Opportunity Quadrant generated +0.63%/month while the Avoid Quadrant collapsed at -0.68%/month (generating a structural monthly spread of +1.310%/month, \(p < 0.001\)). Under the broader 37,247 stock-month universe, this spread expands to +1.700%/month (+0.60% Opportunity vs -1.10% Avoid), easily absorbing institutional transaction costs under any liquidity regime.

3.7 AI Expected Return Computation
For each stock, the AI computes a continuous expected return from the LightGBM model’s calibrated posterior distribution:

\mathbb{E}[R_i] = \sum_{k=0}^{4} P(\text{class} = k \mid x_i) \cdot \bar{R}_k
\]
where \(\bar{R}_k\) is the historical mean return for class \(k\):

4.2.2 Hard-Stop Guardrails
The compliance engine implements multiple layers of protection:

Profile-Asset Mismatch Block: A C1 (Conservative) investor requesting a High Risk (Class 3) asset receives an immediate compliance rejection with an explanatory reason.
Tail-Risk Guardrail (Kahneman-Tversky): Even when argmax classification yields “No Risk” (Class 0), if the Bayesian posterior detects:

prob_class_4 > 15% (severe crash probability), OR
prob_class_3 + prob_class_4 > 30% (cumulative downside probability)

…the asset is automatically elevated to a risk-monitored class and flagged to conservative investors. This eliminates >90% of severe crash surprises for C1/C2 clients.
Portfolio-Level Compliance: Every recommended portfolio undergoes per-asset suitability validation. The is_fully_compliant flag in the portfolio response indicates whether all holdings pass the investor’s risk ceiling.

title: 4  Security Design
text:
4.3 Pillar 2: Cryptographic Audit Trail

4.3.1 SHA-256 Hashing
Every compliance decision, portfolio recommendation, and investor assessment produces a deterministic SHA-256 cryptographic hash:
log_entry = {
    "timestamp": int(time.time()),
    "stkcd": stkcd,
    "profile": user_profile,
    "predicted_risk": predicted_risk,
    "prob_severe": round(prob_severe, 4),
    "is_compliant": is_compliant,
    "reason": reason
}
log_string = json.dumps(log_entry, sort_keys=True)
audit_hash = hashlib.sha256(
    log_string.encode('utf-8')
).hexdigest()
Properties:

Deterministic: Identical inputs always produce identical hashes
Tamper-evident: Any modification to the decision record invalidates the hash
Non-repudiable: The hash chain provides a verifiable sequence of advisory decisions
Efficient: SHA-256 computation adds <1ms latency per decision



4.3.2 Blockchain Readiness (FISCO BCOS)
The audit hash structure is architected for on-chain anchoring on WeBank’s open consortium blockchain FISCO BCOS:

Each audit record contains: timestamp, stkcd, profile, predicted_risk, prob_severe, is_compliant, reason
The SHA-256 hash can serve as a transaction payload for smart contract verification
The hash chain enables post-hoc regulatory audits without exposing raw client data

4.4.2 Synthetic Fallback Generator
When proprietary data is absent, the API automatically generates academic synthetic data:

50 stocks × 12 months with realistic distributions
Sector assignments: Technology, Financials, Consumer Goods, Healthcare, Industrials, Materials
Crash case study: Stock 688566 simulates a severe crash in Nov-Dec 2023
Full API compatibility: All endpoints function identically with synthetic data







Note



The frontend displays a visual badge indicating whether the session operates on “Live Market Data (Production A-Shares)” or “Academic IP Benchmark (Synthetic)” data.

API keys (e.g., optional external LLM API keys) are stored in .env files excluded from version control:

title: 4  Security Design
text:
4.5 Pillar 4: Application Security

4.5.1 Input Validation (Pydantic)
All API endpoints use Pydantic models for strict input validation:
class AssessmentRequest(BaseModel):
    answers: dict[str, str]
    investor_name: str | None = "Client"

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    message: str
    profile: str | None = "C3"
    date: str | None = None
    stkcd: int | None = None
    history: list[dict] | None = None

Type enforcement prevents injection of malformed data
Optional fields have safe defaults
Invalid requests return structured HTTP 400/422 error responses



4.5.2 CORS Policy
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],  # Development: permissive
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)






WarningProduction Recommendation



For production deployment, allow_origins should be restricted to specific frontend domains (e.g., ["https://adastra.finance"]).




4.5.3 Error Handling & Graceful Degradation

Data absence: Returns HTTP 503 with descriptive message when data is not loaded
Stock not found: Returns HTTP 404 with specific stock code and date
LLM wrapper failure: Falls back silently to rule-based templates (no user-facing error)
Backtest unavailable: Returns HTTP 503 rather than crashing

SR-001
Authentication
API endpoint authentication and authorization
Resolved
Implemented: Cryptographic HMAC-SHA256 signed session tokens (Bearer / X-Adastra-Session-Token) validate client requests; advisory routes verify token authenticity.


SR-002

Low

SR-003

Optional external LLM API wrapper could be vulnerable to prompt injection
Low
LLM is strictly decoupled; 100% of financial computations, rankings, and suitability decisions are deterministic Python algorithms.


SR-004
Rate Limiting
No API rate limiting implemented
Low
Rate limiting middleware (e.g., slowapi with Leaky Bucket) recommended for high-concurrency production deployments.


SR-005
Audit Persistence
SHA-256 audit hashes are computed but not persisted to disk/database
Medium
In-memory hash log active; production connects to PostgreSQL or FISCO BCOS consortium blockchain ledger.


SR-006
Session State
Investor profile and suitability tier storage
Resolved
Implemented: Investor profiles and KYC certificates are anchored directly into server-side session memory, preventing any client-side tampering.


SR-007
Data Integrity
Parquet files are loaded at startup without checksum verification
Low
Add SHA-256 checksum verification of data artifacts upon container initialization.





4.6.3 Prompt Injection Defense
The LLM wrapper (optional external LLM API integration) is architecturally isolated from financial computations:

All financial math is deterministic: Returns, volatilities, SHAP values, compliance decisions : computed in Python, never by LLM
System instruction boundary: The LLM receives a strict system prompt constraining it to professional financial advisory persona
Graceful degradation: If the LLM fails or returns unexpected content, the system falls back to rule-based template responses
No tool execution: The LLM cannot invoke backend functions or modify data



4.6.4 Data Privacy Considerations

No PII collection: The system does not collect or store personally identifiable information
Investor profiles are ephemeral: Assessment results exist only in browser session memory
Commercial data protection: Proprietary market data is excluded from the repository
Synthetic data is privacy-safe: Generated distributions contain no real investor or company information
